def: Structured data fits a fixed schema of rows and columns, like a relational table. Semi-structured data has some organization, like tags or key-value pairs, but no fixed schema, like JSON or XML. Unstructured data has no predefined organization at all, like images, video, or free-form text.
eg: The exam tests whether you can classify a described dataset into one of these three buckets — JSON and XML are the classic semi-structured examples to remember.

def: A workload optimized for many short, fast read/write transactions, like inserting an order or updating a customer record — the backbone of day-to-day operational applications.
eg: Think of OLTP as the system running the business minute to minute: e-commerce checkouts, ATM withdrawals, booking systems.

def: A workload optimized for complex analytical queries over large volumes of historical data, aggregating and summarizing for reporting and business intelligence rather than fast single-record transactions.
eg: OLAP is the analytics side: think data warehouses and Power BI reports built on years of aggregated sales data, not a single order lookup.

def: Relational databases store data in tables with a fixed schema and relationships enforced through keys, queried with SQL. Non-relational (NoSQL) databases store data in flexible formats, like documents, key-value pairs, or graphs, built for scale and schema flexibility over strict structure.
eg: Neither type is universally the better choice — the exam wants you to match the data shape and consistency needs of a scenario to the right category.

def: CSV: plain-text, row-based, human readable. JSON: semi-structured, key-value, widely used for APIs. Parquet and ORC: columnar binary formats optimized for compression and analytics. Avro: row-based binary format popular for streaming data with an embedded schema.
eg: Columnar formats like Parquet are the answer whenever a scenario stresses fast analytical queries over just a few columns of a huge dataset.

def: A Database Administrator (DBA) provisions, secures, monitors, and maintains databases. A Data Engineer designs and builds data pipelines and storage systems that move and transform data. A Data Analyst explores data and builds reports and visualizations to support business decisions.
eg: If a scenario is about building an ETL pipeline, that is a Data Engineer; if it is about building a dashboard, that is a Data Analyst; if it is about backups and performance tuning, that is a DBA.

def: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — the guarantees a relational database transaction provides: a transaction either fully completes or fully fails, data stays valid, concurrent transactions do not interfere with each other, and committed changes survive a crash.
eg: ACID is closely associated with relational, OLTP-style databases; many NoSQL stores trade some of these guarantees for scale and flexibility.

term: The four V's of big data
def: Volume (amount of data), Velocity (speed data arrives and must be processed), Variety (different data types and formats), and Veracity (trustworthiness and quality of the data) — the characteristics commonly used to describe big data workloads.
eg: A scenario mentioning huge volumes arriving continuously from many different source formats, some of uncertain quality, is describing all four V's at once.

term: Database vs. data warehouse vs. data lake
def: A database stores day-to-day operational data. A data warehouse stores large volumes of structured, cleaned, historical data organized for reporting and analytics. A data lake stores massive amounts of raw data of any type before it is necessarily processed.
eg: A data lake accepts data before it is necessarily structured; a data warehouse expects data to already be modeled and cleaned before it arrives.

def: The standard language for defining, querying, and managing data in a relational database, covering data definition (creating tables), data manipulation (inserting, updating, deleting rows), and data queries (retrieving rows with SELECT).
eg: DP-900 expects you to recognize SQL's purpose and the general DDL/DML/query distinction conceptually, not to write complex T-SQL yourself.

def: The overall practice of managing data quality, access, ownership, and compliance across an organization — deciding who can see what data, ensuring it stays accurate, and tracking where it came from.
eg: Roles like a data steward or data owner exist specifically to carry out data governance responsibilities day to day, rather than governance being an abstract policy with no one actually responsible for it.

def: Microsoft's unified data governance service for discovering, cataloging, classifying, and tracking the lineage of data across an organization's estate — the concrete Azure tool that puts data governance into practice rather than leaving it as policy alone.
eg: A data map that shows which sensitive columns live in which database, and where that data flowed from, is a Purview capability, not something a database engine tracks on its own.

def: A data professional role focused on building, training, and evaluating machine learning and statistical models from data to generate predictions or insights — distinct from the reporting focus of a Data Analyst and the day-to-day upkeep handled by a Database Administrator.
eg: If a scenario is about training a model to predict an outcome, that's a Data Scientist; if it's about a dashboard, that's still a Data Analyst.

def: Schema-on-write validates and applies a fixed schema before data is ever stored, the approach a relational database takes. Schema-on-read stores data as-is and applies structure only when it's later queried, the approach a data lake uses so raw files of any shape can land first and get modeled afterward.
eg: A scenario that says structure isn't known until the data is actually read is describing schema-on-read, not a database rejecting badly-formed rows on the way in.

term: Document, key-value, column-family, and graph stores
def: The four common shapes non-relational data takes: document stores hold self-contained JSON-like records, key-value stores pair a simple key with a value for fast lookups, column-family stores group sparse, wide sets of columns for massive write-scale, and graph stores model entities as nodes connected by edges — the model family behind Azure Cosmos DB APIs like the NoSQL, Table, Cassandra, and Gremlin APIs.
eg: Recognizing which of these four shapes a scenario is describing, before even thinking about a specific Azure service, is the first step to picking the right Cosmos DB API.

def: The process of collecting and importing data from one or more source systems into a storage or processing system — the first step before it can be transformed or analyzed, whether it arrives all at once in batches or continuously as a stream.
eg: A nightly file drop into a data lake and a live event feed into a streaming pipeline are both data ingestion — they just differ in which of the two processing patterns they use.

def: The traceable history of a piece of data — where it originated, what systems or transformations it passed through, and where it ultimately landed — so anyone looking at a report can answer where a number actually came from.
eg: Microsoft Purview surfaces lineage automatically as it scans pipelines and data stores, rather than requiring someone to document the data's journey by hand.

def: Tagging data — a column, a file, a whole dataset — according to how sensitive it is, such as public, general, confidential, or highly confidential, so access controls and handling rules can be applied consistently based on that label.
eg: Microsoft Purview can scan a data estate and apply these classifications automatically, flagging columns that look like a credit card number or national ID before a human ever reviews them.

def: A rule describing how long a category of data must be kept before it can be deleted or archived, driven by legal, regulatory, or business requirements rather than by storage cost alone.
eg: A retention policy decides when to act; a mechanism like Blob Storage lifecycle management is what actually carries that decision out automatically.

def: The role responsible for installing, configuring, securing, monitoring, backing up, and tuning databases so they stay available and perform well. On Azure, much of the routine patching and backup work moves to the platform, but the DBA still owns access, performance, and recovery planning.
prompt: The role responsible for installing, configuring, securing, monitoring, backing up, and tuning databases so they stay available and perform well. On Azure, much of the routine patching and backup work moves to the platform, but the _____ still owns access, performance, and recovery planning.
eg: In an exam scenario, backups, user permissions, and slow-query tuning are DBA work. Building pipelines is a Data Engineer task, and building reports is a Data Analyst task.

def: The role that designs, builds, and maintains the pipelines and storage systems that collect, move, clean, and transform data so others can use it. Typical tools include Azure Data Factory, Azure Synapse Analytics, Azure Databricks, and Microsoft Fabric.
eg: If a scenario describes loading raw files into a data lake and transforming them for reporting, the person doing that work is the Data Engineer.

def: The role that explores data and turns it into insight by cleaning and modeling it, then building reports and dashboards in a tool such as Power BI. The goal is to answer business questions for decision makers.
eg: A scenario about building a sales dashboard or a report for managers is a Data Analyst task, while training a predictive model is a Data Scientist task.

def: Any data that can identify a specific person, either by itself or combined with other data, such as a name, email address, national ID number, or phone number. PII usually needs stronger protection and handling under privacy laws.
prompt: Any data that can identify a specific person, either by itself or combined with other data, such as a name, email address, national ID number, or phone number. _____ usually needs stronger protection and handling under privacy laws.
eg: Data classification and masking features exist mainly to find and protect PII, for example by hiding all but the last four digits of a card number.

def: A European Union privacy regulation that governs how organizations collect, store, and process the personal data of people in the EU. It gives individuals rights such as access to their data and its erasure, and applies to any organization handling that data, wherever it is located.
eg: A scenario asking how to show compliance with privacy rules points to governance tools like classification, lineage, and retention policies, which help locate and manage personal data.

term: Encryption at rest vs. encryption in transit
def: Encryption at rest protects data stored on disk, such as database files and blobs. Encryption in transit protects data moving across a network, typically with TLS. Azure encrypts stored data by default and uses secure connections for most services.
eg: Transparent Data Encryption and Storage Service Encryption are at-rest examples. HTTPS and TLS connections are in-transit examples. Know which one a scenario describes.

def: A data owner is the person accountable for a dataset, who decides who may access it and how it may be used. A data steward handles day-to-day quality, definitions, and rules for that data, making sure standards are followed.
eg: Think of the owner as the one who approves access and the steward as the one who maintains accuracy and consistency. Both roles support data governance.

def: A security practice of giving each user, application, or service only the minimum permissions needed to do its job, and nothing more. It limits the damage if an account is compromised or misused.
eg: In data scenarios it means granting read-only access to an analyst who only builds reports, rather than giving administrator rights to the whole database or storage account.

term: Matching Azure data stores to common use cases
def: Relational transactional apps: Azure SQL (Database, Managed Instance, or SQL Server on a VM) or Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL. JSON documents at global scale: Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL. Simple key-value data: Azure Table Storage or Cosmos DB for Table. Images, video, logs, and backups: Blob Storage. A mountable file share: Azure Files. A big-data lake: Data Lake Storage Gen2. A fast in-memory cache: Azure Cache for Redis or its successor, Azure Managed Redis.
eg: Read the scenario for the shape of the data and the access pattern first, then the scale. Complex multi-table joins point to a relational engine; massive scale with a flexible schema points to Cosmos DB.

term: Delimited text, JSON, XML, and BLOB files
def: Delimited text such as CSV, TSV, or fixed-width files stores one record per line with fields split by a delimiter. JSON stores hierarchical objects in braces and collections in brackets, and suits structured and semi-structured data. XML is a tag-based, human-readable format that has largely been superseded by the less verbose JSON. A BLOB (binary large object) is raw binary data such as images, video, audio, and application-specific documents.
eg: Human-readable formats are convenient but are not optimized for storage space or processing speed; that is the job of optimized formats such as Parquet and Avro.

term: Row-based vs. columnar formats: Avro, Parquet, and Delta Lake
def: Avro is a row-based Apache format whose header, stored as JSON, describes the structure of the binary records, which makes it good for compact storage and for moving data over a network. Parquet is a columnar Apache format, the de facto standard for modern lakehouses, that stores each column's data together so queries can read only the columns they need. Delta Lake builds on Parquet with a transaction log for ACID transactions, versioning, and reliable updates.
eg: Whole-record reads and streaming favor row-based Avro; analytics over a few columns of a huge dataset favor columnar Parquet; reliable updates on lake files point to Delta Lake.

term: Key-value vs. document vs. column-family vs. graph databases
def: Key-value databases pair a unique key with a value in any format. Document databases are a specific form of key-value database where the value is a JSON document that the system is optimized to parse and query. Column-family databases store tabular data whose columns are divided into logically related groups called column families. Graph databases store entities as nodes with links, called edges, that define relationships.
eg: Nonrelational databases are often called NoSQL even though some support a variant of the SQL language.

def: A relational database organizes data into tables, where each row represents one record and each column represents one attribute of that record, with every row in a table sharing the same set of columns.
eg: This fixed, tabular shape is what separates relational data from the flexible shape of most non-relational data stores.

def: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table. A foreign key is a column in one table that references the primary key of another table, creating a relationship between the two tables.
eg: Foreign keys are the mechanism that lets relational databases enforce referential integrity between related tables, like Orders and Customers.

def: The process of organizing tables to reduce data redundancy and improve data integrity, typically by splitting data into multiple related tables instead of repeating the same information in one large table.
eg: A repeated customer name and address on every single order row is a normalization smell — that data belongs in its own Customers table, referenced by a foreign key.

def: A fully managed platform-as-a-service (PaaS) relational database in Azure, based on the Microsoft SQL Server engine, with automatic patching, backups, and high availability handled by Microsoft.
eg: This is the go-to answer whenever a scenario wants a modern SQL Server-compatible database with the least possible management overhead.

def: A PaaS deployment option offering near-complete compatibility with on-premises SQL Server, including features like cross-database queries and SQL Server Agent, making it easier to lift-and-shift an existing SQL Server estate into Azure.
eg: Choose Managed Instance over Azure SQL Database when an existing on-premises workload depends on instance-level features that Azure SQL Database does not support.

term: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines
def: An infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS) option that runs full SQL Server inside a customer-managed Azure VM, giving complete control over the OS and SQL Server configuration, at the cost of the customer handling OS patching themselves.
eg: This is the right answer whenever a scenario needs OS-level access or a SQL Server version or feature not available in the PaaS options.

term: Azure Database for PostgreSQL and MySQL
def: Fully managed PaaS offerings for the open-source PostgreSQL and MySQL database engines, giving the same automatic patching, backup, and scaling benefits as Azure SQL Database, for organizations already standardized on those engines.
eg: These exist so teams do not have to migrate off PostgreSQL or MySQL just to get a managed Azure experience.

def: The DTU (Database Transaction Unit) model bundles compute, memory, and storage into fixed performance tiers. The vCore model lets you independently choose compute and storage, and can apply Azure Hybrid Benefit to reuse existing SQL Server licenses.
eg: vCore is the more flexible, and generally more cost-transparent, of the two — and it is the one that supports bringing your own SQL Server license.

def: A separate data structure that lets a database find rows matching a query without scanning every row in a table, at the cost of extra storage and slightly slower writes since the index itself must also be updated.
eg: A primary key column is indexed automatically, and foreign key columns are often worth indexing too, since they are exactly the kind of columns queries filter and join on most often.

def: Deliberately reintroducing redundancy into a table, the opposite of normalization, to reduce the number of joins a read-heavy reporting query needs, at the cost of extra storage and more places to update when the data changes.
eg: A data warehouse's star schema is itself a denormalized design on purpose — fact and dimension tables are shaped for fast aggregation, not for eliminating redundancy the way a normalized OLTP schema is.

def: A shared pool of compute and storage resources that multiple Azure SQL databases draw from together, letting databases with unpredictable, non-simultaneous usage spikes share capacity instead of each being sized and billed for its own worst case. Elastic pools are available under both the DTU and vCore purchasing models.
prompt: A shared pool of compute and storage resources that multiple Azure SQL databases draw from together, letting databases with unpredictable, non-simultaneous usage spikes share capacity instead of each being sized and billed for its own worst case. _____ are available under both the DTU and vCore purchasing models.
eg: Dozens of small databases that each only spike occasionally, and rarely all at once, is the classic signal pointing at an elastic pool instead of provisioning every database for its own peak.

def: A vCore-based Azure SQL Database service tier built for very large or fast-growing databases, supporting rapid storage auto-scaling up to 128 TB with backup and restore times that stay fast regardless of database size, unlike the lower size ceilings of the Standard or General Purpose tiers.
eg: A scenario emphasizing multi-terabyte growth alongside fast restores no matter the size is describing Hyperscale, not just a larger General Purpose database.

def: Active geo-replication keeps up to four readable secondary copies of an Azure SQL Database in other regions. A failover group wraps that replication with a single, stable connection endpoint that automatically redirects the application to the secondary region during an outage, so the application never has to track which region is currently active.
eg: This is what makes Azure SQL Database resilient to a whole regional outage, on top of the automated backups it already takes for point-in-time restore within a single region.

def: Encryption that protects an Azure SQL database's data and log files at rest by encrypting the physical storage itself, enabled by default, with no application changes required and no visible difference to the queries running against the database.
eg: TDE protects data sitting on disk; it does nothing to stop someone with legitimate query access from reading sensitive columns in plain text — that's what Dynamic Data Masking is for.

def: A feature that obscures sensitive column values, like full credit card numbers, in query results for non-privileged users, without changing the actual data stored in the database or requiring every application to add its own masking logic.
eg: Dynamic Data Masking only changes what's returned by a query — a user with the right permissions can still see the unmasked data, so it's a convenience control, not full encryption.

def: A vCore-based compute option that automatically scales compute up and down based on workload demand and can auto-pause during inactive periods, billing by the second for compute actually used instead of for continuously provisioned capacity.
eg: This fits intermittent, unpredictable workloads well — a database sitting idle overnight costs far less than it would on an always-on provisioned tier.

term: SQL statement types: DDL, DML, and DCL
def: Data Definition Language (DDL) creates and changes structures, with CREATE, ALTER, and DROP. Data Manipulation Language (DML) works with the rows, with INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE, and SELECT is often grouped with it. Data Control Language (DCL) manages permissions, with GRANT, REVOKE, and DENY.
eg: A question that shows CREATE TABLE is DDL, one that shows INSERT or UPDATE is DML, and one that shows GRANT is DCL. Match the keyword to the category.

def: Microsoft's extension of standard SQL used by SQL Server, Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance, and Azure Synapse Analytics. It adds programming features such as variables, conditional logic, loops, and error handling to ordinary queries.
eg: T-SQL is the dialect for the Microsoft SQL family. PostgreSQL and MySQL use their own dialects, so a scenario naming T-SQL points to a SQL Server-based service.

def: A JOIN combines rows from two tables based on a related column, usually a foreign key matching a primary key. An INNER JOIN returns only matching rows, while a LEFT OUTER JOIN keeps every row from the left table and fills missing matches with NULL.
eg: Joining Orders to Customers on CustomerID returns each order with its customer name. Normalized designs depend on joins to reassemble data that was split across tables.

def: A view is a virtual table defined by a saved SELECT query. It stores no data of its own, and each time it is queried the underlying tables are read. Views simplify complex queries and can expose only selected columns to certain users.
eg: A view is the answer when a scenario wants to give a team a simplified or restricted window onto tables without copying data or granting access to the base tables.

def: A named, saved set of SQL statements stored in the database and run by calling it, optionally with parameters. They keep logic in one place, can reduce network traffic, and let you grant execute permission without direct table access.
eg: A scenario about reusing the same multi-step logic from many applications, or limiting what apps can do to tables, points to a stored procedure.

def: A trigger is code that runs automatically when a specific event occurs on a table, such as an INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE. It is commonly used to enforce business rules or record changes in an audit table.
eg: The key word is automatic: nobody calls a trigger. A stored procedure runs only when called, while a trigger fires on the data change itself.

def: Rules enforced by the database to keep data valid. Common constraints are PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, and DEFAULT, and they reject changes that would break the rule.
eg: A NOT NULL constraint stops a row without a value in a required column, and a CHECK constraint can restrict a value to a range, like age above zero.

def: A Microsoft ETL tool for building data movement and transformation packages, long used with on-premises SQL Server. Existing packages can run in Azure Data Factory using the Azure-SSIS integration runtime.
prompt: A Microsoft ETL tool for building data movement and transformation packages, long used with on-premises SQL Server. Existing packages can run in Azure Data Factory using the Azure-_____ integration runtime.
eg: A scenario about lifting existing SSIS packages into the cloud without rewriting them points to Azure Data Factory with the Azure-SSIS integration runtime.

term: Azure SQL Database vs. Managed Instance vs. SQL Server on VMs
def: SQL Server on Azure VMs is IaaS: full SQL Server compatibility and full control, but you manage the OS, updates, and backups. SQL Managed Instance is PaaS with near-100 percent SQL Server compatibility, automated updates and backups, and instance pools to share resources across smaller instances. SQL Database is PaaS for new cloud applications, as a single database or an elastic pool, with some instance-level features unavailable.
eg: Lift and shift with full control points to the VM; lift and shift with minimal changes and less administration points to Managed Instance; a new app with minimal instance-level dependencies points to SQL Database.

def: A tool you install to analyze your SQL Server databases and report compatibility issues that could block migration, whether the target is Azure SQL Managed Instance or Azure SQL Database. The Azure Database Migration Service then performs the migration for most databases with minimal code changes. Microsoft retired DMA on July 16, 2025 and now points to its newer migration tooling, but the DP-900 module still names it as the assessment tool.
eg: Run an assessment before choosing the target: it shows whether an on-premises application depends on features that Azure SQL Database does not offer.

term: Flexible server for Azure Database for MySQL and PostgreSQL
def: The flexible-server deployment option is a fully managed database service that gives more granular control over configuration and management functions, plus cost optimization controls. For MySQL it is the recommended option for new workloads, and with an Azure free account flexible server can be used free for 12 months. Azure Database for MySQL is based on the MySQL Community Edition.
eg: MySQL backups keep point-in-time restore for up to 35 days, with 7 days as the default. PostgreSQL adds support for custom data types and extensions, though not every extension is available.

term: Azure SQL Database security, monitoring, and AI features
def: SQL Database encrypts data at rest and in motion, offers advanced threat protection with vulnerability assessments and detection of anomalous activity and SQL injection attempts, writes auditing events to an Azure storage account, and supports point-in-time restore and cross-region replication. It also offers a free offer for new databases and AI assistance that can suggest query optimizations and help troubleshoot performance in natural language.
eg: Threat detection and auditing sit on top of the built-in availability guarantees; they do not replace the customer's decisions about permissions and data classification.

def: Microsoft's globally distributed, multi-model NoSQL database service, built for low-latency access at massive scale, with turnkey global distribution and multiple consistency level options.
eg: Cosmos DB is the flagship non-relational answer on this exam whenever a scenario needs global scale with low latency.

def: Cosmos DB supports multiple APIs over the same underlying engine: the API for NoSQL (the native API, formerly called the Core (SQL) API) for JSON documents, the API for MongoDB, the API for Apache Cassandra (column-family), the API for Apache Gremlin (graph data), and the API for Table (key-value).
eg: Picking the right API usually comes down to what your application or existing skill set already uses — the MongoDB API for teams already using MongoDB drivers, Gremlin for graph and relationship-heavy data, and so on.

def: A NoSQL key-value store for large amounts of structured, non-relational data, where each entity is accessed by a partition key and a row key, ideal for fast lookups of simple data at low cost.
eg: Table Storage is a simpler, cheaper alternative to using Cosmos DB's Table API when global distribution or guaranteed low-latency SLAs are not required.

def: Object storage for large amounts of unstructured data, like images, video, log files, and backups, organized into containers, with access tiers (Hot, Cool, Cold, Archive) to balance storage cost against retrieval speed.
eg: Blob Storage is the default answer for storing unstructured files at scale in Azure.

def: Fully managed file shares in the cloud, accessible via the standard SMB and NFS protocols, so they can be mounted concurrently by multiple VMs or on-premises machines just like a traditional network file share.
eg: Azure Files is the answer whenever a scenario wants a lift-and-shift replacement for an on-premises file server, not just object storage for an application.

def: A set of capabilities built on top of Azure Blob Storage that adds a hierarchical namespace (real directories and folders) and fine-grained access control, purpose-built for large-scale big data analytics workloads.
eg: Data Lake Storage Gen2 is Blob Storage plus a hierarchical namespace — not a separate storage product built from scratch.

def: Splitting a large dataset across multiple physical nodes or databases, each holding a subset of the rows called a shard, so no single node's storage or throughput becomes a bottleneck as the dataset grows — the physical distribution strategy behind horizontally-scaled stores like Azure Cosmos DB.
eg: Sharding distributes rows across separate machines; it is a different concept from normalization, which reorganizes columns into separate related tables on the same database.

def: A tunable spectrum from strong (every read sees the most recent committed write) to eventual (a read may briefly return stale data), letting Azure Cosmos DB trade off latency and availability against how immediately consistent reads need to be across its globally distributed replicas.
eg: Choosing a weaker consistency level is a deliberate trade for lower latency and higher availability, not a defect — the right level depends on whether an application can tolerate a brief delay before every region sees the same value.

def: The property chosen on each item in an Azure Cosmos DB container that determines which physical partition it's stored in, spreading a container's data and throughput across many nodes — the concrete mechanism Cosmos DB uses to implement sharding, or horizontal partitioning.
eg: A partition key with only a few distinct values concentrates most items onto the same few partitions, defeating the point of choosing one at all.

def: A fully managed, in-memory key-value store built for sub-millisecond caching and session-state lookups, meant to take repeated load off a backend database rather than serve as a durable, long-term primary store the way Azure Cosmos DB or Azure Table Storage does.
eg: Whenever a scenario needs the fastest possible repeated read of the same small piece of data, like a session token, and doesn't need it to persist long-term, this is the answer over a full database service. Azure Cache for Redis Basic, Standard, and Premium instances retire on September 30, 2028, and Microsoft recommends moving to Azure Managed Redis, but the in-memory caching concept being tested is unchanged.

def: The single currency Azure Cosmos DB uses to measure and bill the compute cost of every operation — every read, write, and query consumes some number of Request Units, and a container's throughput is provisioned, or scaled automatically, in RU/s rather than in raw CPU or memory.
prompt: The single currency Azure Cosmos DB uses to measure and bill the compute cost of every operation — every read, write, and query consumes some number of _____, and a container's throughput is provisioned, or scaled automatically, in _____ rather than in raw CPU or memory.
eg: A heavier query, like one that scans many items, simply consumes more Request Units per call than a single point read by ID.

def: The options controlling how many copies of Azure Storage data are kept and where. LRS (locally redundant storage) keeps copies within one datacenter. ZRS (zone-redundant storage) spreads copies across availability zones in one region. GRS (geo-redundant storage) also replicates asynchronously to a second, distant region. RA-GRS adds read access to that secondary region's copy.
eg: Each step up — LRS to ZRS to GRS to RA-GRS — buys more resilience against a larger failure, at a higher cost.

def: A persistent, ordered log of every insert and update made to a Cosmos DB container, which downstream applications or functions can read to react to data changes as they happen, without polling the container or re-querying for what changed.
eg: A function that sends a notification the moment a new order document is written is a typical change feed consumer — it reacts to the stream of changes instead of repeatedly asking the container whether anything changed yet.

def: A Cosmos DB configuration where more than one region can accept write operations at the same time, rather than all writes going through a single primary region, reducing write latency for users close to each writable region and improving availability if one region goes down.
eg: The alternative, single-region writes, sends every write to one primary region no matter where the client is, while still allowing the other regions to serve reads.

def: Rule-based policies that automatically move blobs between access tiers, like Hot to Cool to Archive, or delete them outright, based on conditions like how long it's been since a blob was last modified or accessed — carrying out a data retention policy without manual intervention.
eg: Rules like this are what actually save money from access tiers in practice — few teams manually re-tier files one by one as they age.

def: A common way to organize a data lake into progressive layers: the bronze zone holds raw, unprocessed data as it was ingested, the silver zone holds cleaned and validated data, and the gold zone holds highly refined, business-ready data modeled for reporting.
eg: Data generally only flows one direction through these zones, bronze to silver to gold, with each stage adding more structure and trustworthiness on top of the previous one.

def: The native API of Azure Cosmos DB, which stores data as JSON documents and is queried with a SQL-like query language. It was formerly called the Core (SQL) API and offers the full range of Cosmos DB features.
eg: Pick it for new document-based applications with no existing database to match. Choose another API only when a scenario names an existing MongoDB, Cassandra, Gremlin, or Table workload.

def: An API that lets applications written for MongoDB use Azure Cosmos DB, keeping existing MongoDB drivers and tools. Data is stored as documents, so it suits workloads with flexible, JSON-like data.
eg: A scenario about migrating an existing MongoDB application to Azure with minimal code changes points to this API.

term: Azure Cosmos DB for Apache Gremlin
def: The Cosmos DB API for graph data, where data is stored as vertices (entities) and edges (relationships) and queried with the Gremlin traversal language. It is built for highly connected data.
eg: Social networks, recommendation engines, and fraud detection, where the relationships matter as much as the entities, are the classic graph scenarios.

term: Cosmos DB throughput modes: provisioned, autoscale, and serverless
def: Provisioned throughput reserves a fixed number of RU/s that you set. Autoscale adjusts provisioned RU/s automatically between a minimum and maximum based on usage. Serverless has no reservation and bills only for the Request Units your operations consume.
eg: Serverless fits intermittent or unpredictable traffic, autoscale fits variable workloads, and standard provisioned throughput fits steady, predictable load.

term: Cosmos DB resource hierarchy: account, database, container, item
def: A Cosmos DB account is the unit of global distribution. It holds databases, a database holds containers, and a container holds items. The container is the unit of scalability and is where the partition key is defined.
eg: Depending on the API, an item is a document, row, node, or edge. Throughput can be provisioned on a container or shared across a database.

def: Block blobs hold text and binary files and are the common choice for documents, images, and video. Append blobs are optimized for adding data to the end, such as log files. Page blobs support random read and write access and back Azure VM disks.
eg: Unless a scenario mentions continuously appended logs or VM disks, the answer for stored files is block blobs.

def: In Azure Table Storage, each entity is identified by a PartitionKey and a RowKey together. The PartitionKey groups related entities in the same partition, and the RowKey is unique within that partition.
eg: Queries that specify both keys are the fastest because they go straight to one entity. Scanning across many partitions is slower.

def: The top-level container for Azure Storage services. A single account provides a unique namespace for Blob storage, Azure Files, Queue storage, and Table storage, and you choose its performance tier and redundancy option when you create it.
eg: Services like Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 are not separate products. They are enabled on a storage account by turning on the hierarchical namespace.

def: Strong means every read reflects the most recent write. Bounded staleness lets reads lag by a configurable time or number of versions. Session guarantees consistency within one client session and is the most widely used level, and the recommended starting point for most transactional apps. Consistent prefix never shows out-of-order writes but can be stale. Eventual is the weakest guarantee with the highest availability.
eg: Strong at one end and Eventual at the other, with three intermediate levels. A weaker level is a deliberate trade for latency and availability.

term: Cosmos DB partitions, shared throughput, and serverless limits
def: A logical partition can hold up to 20 GB of data, so a partition key with many distinct, evenly used values matters. Throughput can be dedicated to one container or shared at the database level across up to 25 containers. A serverless account is limited to a single Azure region, so global distribution needs provisioned throughput instead.
eg: Cosmos DB indexes every property by default and is schema-agnostic: items in one container do not need the same properties.

term: When to use Cosmos DB, and when not to
def: A strong fit for IoT and telemetry ingestion, gaming profiles and leaderboards, retail catalogs and carts, and web and mobile apps that need flexible schema, global reach, and consistent low latency. A poor fit for workloads that depend on complex multi-table joins, where Azure SQL Database is better, and for large-scale historical analytics, where Microsoft Fabric or Azure Synapse Analytics are better.
eg: Cosmos DB for NoSQL also supports Fabric mirroring, which replicates operational data into Fabric so analytics does not load the transactional workload.

term: Cosmos DB for Table and for Apache Cassandra
def: Cosmos DB for Table stores key-value pairs with the same programming model as Azure Table Storage, adding greater scalability, global distribution, automatic secondary indexes, and instant autoscale. Cosmos DB for Apache Cassandra suits teams migrating a Cassandra workload, using the CQL query language over column-family tables whose rows need not share the same columns.
eg: Azure Table Storage is still available and supported, but Cosmos DB for Table is the recommended choice for new key-value workloads at scale.

term: Blob tier minimum stays and rehydration
def: To avoid early deletion penalties, data should stay in Cool for at least 30 days, Cold for at least 90, and Archive for at least 180. Hot, Cool, and Cold are online and read in milliseconds. Archive blobs are offline: to read one you change its tier to Hot, Cool, or Cold and wait for rehydration, which can take up to 15 hours.
eg: Lifecycle management policies can move blobs Hot to Cool to Cold to Archive by days since modification, and delete them when they are outdated.

def: Azure Files offers managed cloud file shares over SMB, which works from Windows, Linux, and macOS, and NFS, which is for Linux. An NFS share needs an SSD-tier storage account plus a virtual network that controls access. A single file can be up to 4 TiB, and shares come in an HDD tier and a faster, costlier SSD tier. Azure File Sync can keep local Windows Server caches in step with a share.
eg: Choose Azure Files when applications expect a traditional network file share; choose Blob Storage for object storage accessed through an API.

term: Data Lake Storage Gen2 hierarchical namespace and ACLs
def: Data Lake Storage Gen2 is enabled by turning on the hierarchical namespace option of a storage account, either at creation or by upgrading an existing account, and the upgrade is one-way: it cannot be reverted to a flat namespace. The hierarchy also enables POSIX-compliant access control lists to set read, write, and execute permissions on individual files and folders, separate from Azure RBAC.
eg: Microsoft Fabric's OneLake is built on top of Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, and Azure Databricks can mount a Data Lake Storage Gen2 file system to process huge volumes of data.

def: The successor to Azure Cache for Redis, an in-memory key-value service for caching and session state. All Azure Cache for Redis Basic, Standard, and Premium instances remain available until they retire on September 30, 2028, and Microsoft recommends upgrading them to Azure Managed Redis.
prompt: The successor to Azure Cache for Redis, an in-memory key-value service for caching and session state. All Azure Cache for Redis Basic, Standard, and Premium instances remain available until they retire on September 30, 2028, and Microsoft recommends upgrading them to _____.
eg: The tested concept is unchanged: an in-memory cache offloads repeated reads from a database but is not a durable primary store.

def: A data warehouse stores large volumes of structured, historical data optimized for reporting. A star schema organizes that data into a central fact table (measurable events, like sales) surrounded by dimension tables (descriptive context, like product, customer, or date).
eg: Fact tables hold the numbers you aggregate; dimension tables hold the descriptive labels you slice and filter by.

def: ETL (Extract, Transform, Load) transforms data before loading it into the destination store. ELT (Extract, Load, Transform) loads raw data into the destination first and transforms it afterward, taking advantage of the destination's own compute power.
eg: Modern cloud-scale analytics, including tools like Azure Synapse and Databricks, increasingly favor ELT because the destination often has more processing power than a separate transform step.

def: Batch processing collects and processes data in large groups on a schedule, like a nightly job. Streaming, or real-time, processing processes data continuously as each event arrives, with results available within seconds or less.
eg: A scenario asking for second-level insight as events happen is streaming; a scenario processing an entire day's transactions overnight is batch.

def: A unified analytics service combining big data and data warehousing, offering serverless and dedicated SQL pools for querying data, along with built-in Apache Spark pools, in a single workspace.
eg: Synapse is the answer whenever a scenario wants one platform that spans data warehousing, big data (Spark), and pipeline orchestration together. It remains supported, though Microsoft now positions Microsoft Fabric (and Azure Databricks) as the platforms for large-scale analytics, and the current DP-900 study guide names Databricks and Fabric rather than Synapse.

def: A cloud-based data integration service for building, scheduling, and orchestrating ETL/ELT pipelines that move and transform data between many different source and destination systems.
eg: Data Factory is about moving and orchestrating data, not analyzing it directly — think of it as the plumbing that feeds a data warehouse or data lake.

def: An Apache Spark-based analytics platform, optimized for large-scale data engineering, data science, and machine learning workloads, offered as a first-party Azure service.
eg: Databricks is the go-to answer for big-data processing and machine learning at scale, distinct from Synapse's broader warehouse-plus-everything scope.

def: A fully managed real-time analytics service for processing and analyzing streaming data, such as telemetry from IoT devices or clickstream data, as it arrives, using a SQL-like query language.
eg: Stream Analytics is the dedicated real-time processing answer, as distinct from Data Factory, which is built for scheduled, batch-style orchestration.

def: An end-to-end, software-as-a-service analytics platform that unifies data engineering, data integration, data warehousing, data science, and Power BI on top of a single shared data lake called OneLake.
eg: Fabric is the newest, most consolidated answer — think of it as bringing Synapse, Data Factory, and Power BI together under one SaaS umbrella with one copy of the data in OneLake.

def: A business intelligence suite for connecting to data sources, modeling data, and building interactive reports and dashboards, made up of Power BI Desktop (authoring), the Power BI Service (publishing and sharing), and Power BI Mobile.
prompt: A business intelligence suite for connecting to data sources, modeling data, and building interactive reports and dashboards, made up of _____ Desktop (authoring), the _____ Service (publishing and sharing), and _____ Mobile.
eg: Power BI typically sits on top of a data warehouse, data lake, or another data source to turn it into interactive reports and dashboards.

term: Import vs. DirectQuery mode in Power BI
def: Import mode copies data into Power BI's own fast in-memory model for the best query performance, refreshed periodically on a schedule. DirectQuery leaves the data in its source system and queries it live on each interaction, trading some performance for always-current data.
eg: DirectQuery is the right choice when data must always reflect the live source; Import mode is the right choice when speed matters most and slightly stale data is acceptable.

def: An architecture combining a data lake’s low-cost, flexible storage for any file type with a data warehouse’s structured, query-optimized layer on top — one platform for both raw and curated data instead of maintaining two separate systems.
eg: Microsoft Fabric is built around exactly this lakehouse pattern, unifying what used to be a separate data lake and a separate data warehouse into one workspace.

def: A fact table stores the numeric, measurable events at the center of a star schema — like a sales amount or a quantity sold. Dimension tables store the descriptive context around those facts — product, customer, date — used to filter and group them.
eg: This is exactly the split at the heart of a star schema — the fact table is what you aggregate; the dimension tables are what you slice and filter by.

term: Serverless SQL pool vs. dedicated SQL pool
def: A serverless SQL pool in Azure Synapse Analytics bills per query based on data processed, with no infrastructure to provision ahead of time. A dedicated SQL pool provisions and bills for continuously-running compute, sized in advance for predictable, heavy workloads.
eg: Ad hoc, unpredictable exploration favors serverless (pay only when you actually query); a large, steady reporting workload favors dedicated, since its provisioned compute is cheaper per-query at real scale.

def: A fast, fully managed big-data analytics service purpose-built for ad hoc, interactive exploration of huge volumes of time-stamped log, telemetry, and event data, queried with the Kusto Query Language (KQL) rather than needing to be pre-modeled into a star schema first.
eg: Contrast this with Azure Synapse Analytics: Data Explorer is optimized specifically for fast log and telemetry exploration, not general-purpose data warehousing.

def: A big-data streaming ingestion service that can receive and buffer millions of events per second from applications and devices, acting as the front door that feeds a downstream processor like Azure Stream Analytics.
eg: Event Hubs ingests and buffers the stream; Azure Stream Analytics is the separate engine that actually queries and analyzes it as it flows through.

def: A dataset (now officially called a semantic model) is the data model a Power BI report queries, built from one or more connected sources. A dataflow is a reusable set of data preparation logic, built with Power Query, that can feed multiple datasets so the same cleanup steps aren't rebuilt inside every individual report.
eg: A dataflow sits upstream of a dataset (semantic model) — it's where shared transformation logic lives once, instead of being copy-pasted into every report that needs it.

def: A report is a multi-page set of interactive visualizations built against one dataset (semantic model). A dashboard is a single page of tiles pinned from one or more reports, often from different datasets entirely, built for at-a-glance monitoring rather than the deeper exploration a report supports.
eg: A dashboard can mix tiles pinned from several different reports; a report itself is always tied to just the one dataset behind it.

def: A data integration and orchestration capability built directly into an Azure Synapse Analytics workspace, sharing the same underlying engine as Azure Data Factory, so pipelines can move and transform data without needing a separate Data Factory resource alongside Synapse.
eg: This is why a team already living inside a Synapse workspace doesn't necessarily need to stand up Azure Data Factory separately just to orchestrate data movement.

def: A capability that connects an operational store, like Azure Cosmos DB or Azure SQL Database, directly to Azure Synapse Analytics for near real-time analytics over operational data, without building or running a separate ETL pipeline to copy the data first. For new work, Microsoft now recommends mirroring into Microsoft Fabric as the successor approach to Synapse Link.
eg: This is hybrid transactional/analytical processing (HTAP) in practice — analytical queries run against a near real-time copy of operational data, instead of waiting on a nightly batch pipeline to catch up.

def: The compute infrastructure Azure Data Factory uses to actually execute a pipeline's activities. The Azure integration runtime handles cloud-to-cloud data movement. The self-hosted integration runtime, installed on a machine inside a private network, connects to data stores that aren't reachable from the public internet, like an on-premises database. The Azure-SSIS integration runtime runs lifted-and-shifted SQL Server Integration Services packages.
eg: A pipeline that needs to pull data out of an on-premises SQL Server behind a firewall needs the self-hosted integration runtime — the regular Azure integration runtime has no way to reach into that private network.

def: A feature of Azure Synapse Analytics dedicated SQL pools that lets T-SQL queries read data sitting in external storage, like files in a data lake, through an external table, without first loading or copying that data into the data warehouse.
eg: This is what lets a warehouse query raw data lake files directly, rather than requiring a full load step before any SQL can touch them.

def: Time-based groupings, like tumbling, hopping, and sliding windows, that Azure Stream Analytics uses to aggregate a continuous stream of events over a defined time interval, such as counting events every 5 minutes, since a stream has no natural end point to aggregate over otherwise.
eg: A tumbling window is fixed-length and non-overlapping, like every distinct 5-minute block in a row, which is the simplest window type to picture first before layering on hopping or sliding variants.

def: An open-source distributed processing engine that splits large data processing jobs across many machines and keeps data in memory for speed. It supports batch and streaming workloads and languages such as Python, Scala, and SQL.
eg: Azure Databricks, Synapse Spark pools, and Microsoft Fabric all run Spark. A scenario about large-scale data transformation or machine learning on big data points to Spark.

def: Interactive documents that combine runnable code cells, their output, and explanatory text. Data engineers and data scientists use them in Microsoft Fabric, Azure Databricks, and Synapse to explore data and run Spark code step by step.
eg: A notebook is the right tool for exploratory analysis and iterative data preparation. A Data Factory pipeline is the tool for scheduled, repeatable orchestration.

def: The single, unified data lake built into every Microsoft Fabric tenant, often described as OneDrive for data. Fabric items such as lakehouses and warehouses store their tables there automatically in Delta Parquet format.
eg: Each tenant has exactly one OneLake. Shortcuts let it reference data in other locations, such as ADLS Gen2, without copying it.

def: The Fabric workload for streaming and event data. Eventstreams capture and route events, an Eventhouse with a KQL database stores and queries time-based data, and real-time dashboards visualize it, with alerts and automated actions available through Activator (formerly Data Activator).
eg: For streaming scenarios in Fabric, this is the Fabric-native counterpart to Azure Event Hubs plus Azure Stream Analytics and Azure Data Explorer.

def: An open-source storage layer that adds ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and versioning to Parquet files in a data lake. It is the default table format in Microsoft Fabric and Azure Databricks.
eg: Delta tables are what let a data lake behave like a reliable database, which is why the lakehouse pattern depends on them.

def: The data connection and transformation tool in Power BI, Excel, and dataflows. It lets you connect to many sources and clean and reshape data, such as removing columns, changing types, and merging tables, through a visual interface before loading it.
eg: Power Query prepares the data before it is loaded. DAX then calculates on the model afterward.

def: The formula language of Power BI semantic models. It is used to create measures, calculated columns, and calculated tables, with Excel-like functions that can aggregate data and respect filters.
eg: A measure like Total Sales is written in DAX and recalculates as users filter a report. Power Query shapes the data, and DAX computes on it.

term: Data Factory pipelines, activities, and linked services
def: A pipeline is a logical group of activities that together perform a task. An activity is a single processing step, like copying data or running a data flow. A linked service defines the connection information to a data store or compute resource.
eg: A pipeline can be started on a schedule or by an event trigger. Think of linked services as the connection strings and activities as the steps.

term: Types of analytics: descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, prescriptive
def: Descriptive analytics shows what happened. Diagnostic analytics explains why it happened. Predictive analytics uses data and models to forecast what will happen. Prescriptive analytics recommends what action to take.
eg: Match the question being asked: a monthly sales summary is descriptive, root-cause analysis of a sales drop is diagnostic, a forecast is predictive, and a suggested action is prescriptive.

def: Bar and column charts compare categories, line charts show trends over time, pie and donut charts show parts of a whole, and scatter plots show the relationship between two numeric values. Maps show geographic data, and cards show a single key number.
eg: Match the visual to the question: use a line chart for sales over months and a card for a single total. A table or matrix is best when exact values matter.

term: Lakehouse vs. warehouse in Microsoft Fabric
def: A Fabric lakehouse stores files and tables in OneLake and is worked on mainly with Spark, with a read-only SQL analytics endpoint for queries. A Fabric warehouse is a full T-SQL data warehouse that supports reads, writes, and transactions.
eg: Spark-first data engineering and mixed or unstructured data point to a lakehouse. T-SQL-centric reporting with stored procedures and views points to a warehouse.

term: Large-scale analytics architecture: ingest, store, model, visualize
def: Data from transactional stores, files, and real-time streams is ingested and processed with ETL or ELT into an analytical store: a relational data warehouse, a file-based data lake, or a hybrid lakehouse. A data model, today usually a semantic model, makes the data easy to report on, and visualizations such as reports and dashboards sit on top. AI assistance, such as Copilot in Fabric, now helps write DAX, SQL, and summaries.
eg: The two leading Azure platforms for this architecture are Microsoft Fabric, a unified SaaS workspace on OneLake, and Azure Databricks, a Spark-based platform on Delta Lake.

def: A shortcut is a live reference to external storage, such as Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, or another OneLake location, that makes the data appear inside a Fabric lakehouse without copying it. No pipeline, no movement, and no duplication.
eg: Use a shortcut when data must stay where it is for compliance or cost reasons but still needs to be queried from Fabric.

def: Mirroring continuously replicates an external database, such as Azure SQL Database, Snowflake, or Azure Cosmos DB, into OneLake in near real time. You configure the source connection once and Fabric handles change tracking, with no pipeline authoring. The data lands in Delta format and can be queried through the lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint.
eg: Mirroring is the recommended successor to Azure Synapse Link for running analytics over operational data without loading the source system.

term: Fabric Data Factory: pipelines and Dataflows Gen2
def: Fabric Data Factory is the recommended starting point for pipeline-based ingestion in Fabric. Pipelines orchestrate multi-step data movement and transformation by chaining activities. Dataflows Gen2 is a low-code, visual way to build reusable transformation logic with Power Query and no code. Azure Data Factory is the standalone service for pipelines outside Fabric, such as to an Azure SQL Database or on-premises sources.
eg: Both use the same pipeline model of activities, datasets, and linked services, so skills transfer. Fabric Notebooks, powered by Spark, cover cases where no built-in connector exists.

def: Eventstream connects to streaming sources such as Azure Event Hubs, Apache Kafka, Azure IoT Hub, and custom endpoints, then routes, filters, and transforms the events before landing them in a Fabric lakehouse, a KQL database, or another Real-Time Intelligence destination.
eg: It is the ingestion front door of Real-Time Intelligence, comparable to Event Hubs plus a light transformation step.

term: Eventhouse, KQL, Real-Time dashboards, Activator, and the real-time hub
def: An Eventhouse is a database optimized for time-series and event data and queried with Kusto Query Language (KQL). Real-Time dashboards visualize live data, Activator triggers automated actions or alerts when streaming data meets conditions, and the real-time hub is a central catalog for discovering and sharing streaming data across the organization.
eg: Together with Eventstreams these make up Real-Time Intelligence in Microsoft Fabric. Activator was formerly called Data Activator.

def: A library built into Apache Spark that treats a live stream as a table that keeps growing: connect to a streaming source such as Event Hubs, read the events into a dataframe, write a query such as a count per minute or a running average, and write results to a sink. It runs on Azure Databricks and Microsoft Fabric.
eg: A good choice when you already use Spark and want to extend it to real-time data. Combined with Delta Lake, one table can be both a streaming sink and a batch source.

term: Event Hubs, IoT Hub, and Kafka as stream sources
def: Azure Event Hubs ingests very high volumes of events, delivers events within a partition in order, and guarantees at-least-once delivery. Azure IoT Hub is similar but optimized for managing event data from Internet-of-things devices. Apache Kafka is an open-source ingestion solution commonly used with Apache Spark. Data Lake Storage Gen2 can also act as a source.
eg: Results are written to sinks such as Event Hubs, Data Lake Storage Gen2, OneLake, Blob storage, Azure SQL Database, Azure Databricks, Fabric, or Power BI.

term: Batch vs. streaming: scope, size, latency, and analysis
def: Batch processing can work on all the data in a dataset, handles large volumes efficiently, typically has latency of hours, and is used for complex analytics. Streaming typically sees only the most recent data or a rolling time window, processes individual records or micro-batches, has latency of seconds or milliseconds, and is used for simple responses, aggregates, and rolling averages.
eg: Many solutions mix both, and an error in one batch input can stop the whole batch run.

def: Lambda architecture combines a batch path that periodically processes data for historical analysis with a stream path that prepares data for real-time views. Delta architectures also combine batch and streaming processing. Kappa is a simpler alternative that removes the separate batch layer by treating all data as a continuous stream and replaying it when historical reprocessing is needed.
eg: Microsoft Fabric and Apache Kafka make kappa-style solutions increasingly practical, but the exam only expects you to recognize these patterns.

term: Azure Databricks building blocks: Unity Catalog, SQL, and Genie
def: Databricks Lakehouse is a unified storage layer on Delta Lake for SQL analytics and machine learning. Databricks SQL is a serverless SQL warehouse for analytical queries. Notebooks hold collaborative Python, SQL, Scala, and R code. Unity Catalog governs data and AI assets with access control, lineage, and discovery. Genie lets users ask natural-language questions and generates and runs the SQL.
eg: Choose Databricks for code-first Spark workflows, multicloud portability, or existing Spark expertise.

def: A declarative framework in Azure Databricks for building reliable, incrementally updated pipelines on Delta Lake. You define what the output tables should contain, and Databricks handles execution order, dependency tracking, and incremental processing. It is the recommended approach for production, continuously running ingestion pipelines.
eg: Databricks Notebooks suit ad-hoc or exploratory ingestion, and can be scheduled as jobs or embedded in a pipeline.

def: When you create a Fabric lakehouse, a SQL analytics endpoint is created automatically so the Delta tables in OneLake can be queried with T-SQL. A Fabric warehouse is a fully managed, SQL Server-compatible warehouse that also stores its data in OneLake.
prompt: When you create a Fabric lakehouse, a _____ is created automatically so the Delta tables in OneLake can be queried with T-SQL. A Fabric warehouse is a fully managed, SQL Server-compatible warehouse that also stores its data in OneLake.
eg: A lakehouse suits mixed or semi-structured data and Spark or machine-learning work; a warehouse suits structured data, SQL teams, strong schema enforcement, and many concurrent users.

def: A Power BI storage mode that lets a semantic model query Delta tables in OneLake directly, combining the speed of in-memory analysis with the scale of a data lake, without a separate import step or scheduled refresh.
eg: Import copies data into Power BI and needs refreshes; DirectQuery queries the source live on each interaction; Direct Lake reads lake files directly.

term: Semantic models, measures, dimensions, and hierarchies
def: An analytical model, called a semantic model in Fabric and Power BI, is built from related tables. It defines measures, the numeric values to analyze, and dimensions, the entities used to aggregate them. Hierarchies let users drill up and down, such as year to month to day. Power BI stores the model in a columnar in-memory store using the VertiPaq engine and calculates aggregations at query time.
eg: Older cubes pre-aggregated values across dimensions using technologies such as SQL Server Analysis Services Multidimensional; the semantic model is the preferred approach today.

def: In a star schema a fact table relates directly to one or more dimension tables. In a snowflake schema the dimension tables relate further to other detail tables, such as a Category table linked to a Product table.
eg: Most analytical models also include a Time dimension so measures can be aggregated across periods.

term: Power BI Desktop, service, and mobile app
def: Power BI Desktop is a Windows application for importing data, building the data model, and creating reports. You publish to the Power BI service, a cloud service where users view and interact with reports, schedule refreshes, and share. The service allows only basic modeling and report editing in a browser, and the Power BI phone app consumes reports, dashboards, and apps.
eg: In Fabric, Power BI content lives in workspaces alongside other items, all backed by OneLake.

term: Copilot and AI visuals in Power BI
def: Copilot in Power BI can summarize a report, create report pages and pick chart types, and generate DAX measures from a natural-language description; it requires Fabric capacity (F2 or higher) or Power BI Premium (P1 or higher). AI visuals include smart narratives, which write a text summary that updates as data changes, the Q&A visual, key influencers, which show the factors that most drive a metric, and the decomposition tree for interactive drill-down.
eg: In Azure Databricks the comparable natural-language experience is Genie, which generates and runs SQL over Delta Lake data.

term: SQL database and Cosmos DB in Microsoft Fabric
def: Fabric includes databases among its integrated capabilities, including a SQL database and Cosmos DB inside Fabric, alongside Fabric Data Factory, the Lakehouse, the Warehouse, data science, Real-Time Intelligence, Power BI, and governance. Fabric IQ is a workload that gives data in OneLake consistent business meaning for people and AI agents, and is currently in preview.
eg: Do not confuse these with the Azure PaaS databases: the Fabric versions are delivered as part of the SaaS platform with no servers to manage.
